candidate.answerReason: The sidewalk needs 45 cubic feet. One cubic yard supplies 27 cubic feet and two supply 54 cubic feet, so the smallest sufficient whole-yard order is 2.

methods.label: Find the volume and choose a sufficient whole-yard order
methods.explanation:
First express all three dimensions in feet. Since \(1\) foot equals \(12\) inches, the thickness is
\[
\frac{3}{12}=\frac14\text{ foot}.
\]
The sidewalk is a rectangular prism, so its volume is length times width times thickness:
\[
60\cdot3\cdot\frac14=45\text{ cubic feet}.
\]
One yard equals \(3\) feet. Thus a cubic yard is a cube measuring \(3\) feet along each edge and contains
\[
3\cdot3\cdot3=27\text{ cubic feet}.
\]
One cubic yard is insufficient because \(27<45\). Two cubic yards provide \(2\cdot27=54\) cubic feet, which is enough. Therefore the smallest sufficient whole-number order is \(2\) cubic yards, choice A.
methods.levelReason: Uses rectangular-prism volume, elementary unit conversions, and comparison of whole-number orders. No formal ceiling notation is needed.

review.mathematicalCheck: The thickness is 3/12 = 1/4 foot, giving volume 60 × 3 × 1/4 = 45 cubic feet. A cubic yard contains 27 cubic feet, and 27 < 45 ≤ 54 proves that two is the smallest sufficient whole-yard order.
